slides.title: Why ML practitioners need to understand GPUs
slides.body:
You can train a transformer without understanding what's happening under the hood. You can also train it 10× slower than necessary, OOM at sequence length 4096, and have no idea why your batch size of 8 fits but 12 doesn't.

This lesson is the substrate. Three things modern GPUs care about:

1. **Compute units** — tensor cores do the matmul; CUDA cores handle elementwise ops. Different operations hit different units, with very different throughput.
2. **Memory hierarchy** — registers (per-thread) → shared memory (per-SM) → HBM (global). Each tier is ~10× larger and ~10× slower than the next.
3. **Bandwidth** — moving bytes in and out of HBM is often the bottleneck, not arithmetic. A poorly fused kernel can spend 90% of its time waiting on memory.

The practical implication: matmul (compute-bound) and softmax/layernorm (memory-bound) live in different regimes. Optimization tactics differ. FlashAttention's whole point is reducing HBM round-trips by tiling — not making attention any faster arithmetically.

slides.title: Worked example: tuning a small matmul to be compute-bound
slides.body: $1024 \times 1024$ FP16 matmul: $2 \cdot 1024^3 \approx 2 \times 10^9$ FLOPs, reads $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1024^2 \approx 4 \times 10^6$ bytes. Arithmetic intensity = $500$ FLOP/byte. On an A100 (peak 312 TFLOPS FP16, 2 TB/s HBM), the roofline crossover is ~150 FLOP/byte — we're compute-bound. Expected runtime $\approx 2 \times 10^9 / (3 \times 10^{14}) \approx 7\mu s$. cuBLAS achieves ~80% of peak, so ~$9\mu s$ in practice. Smaller matmuls ($128 \times 128$ etc.) have lower intensity + are memory-bound; that's why batching matters.

question.question: Derive the roofline crossover
question.goal: Compute the arithmetic intensity at which compute roof = memory roof on an A100.

steps.prompt: A100 FP16: peak compute $P = 312$ TFLOPS = $3.12 \times 10^{14}$ FLOP/s. HBM bandwidth $B = 2.0$ TB/s = $2 \times 10^{12}$ bytes/s. At what intensity $I^*$ (FLOPs/byte) does compute time = memory time?
Operations with intensity $> I^*$ are compute-bound; $< I^*$ are memory-bound. Where do you spend optimization effort for each?

options: Compute-bound: pick bigger matmul shapes / use Tensor Cores. Memory-bound: fuse kernels, tile in shared memory, reduce data movement.

hints: Roofline tells you which roof you're hitting.
steps.reveal: Compute-bound: optimize FLOP throughput. Memory-bound: fuse + tile to reduce HBM traffic.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{I^* = P/B \approx 156 \text{ FLOP/byte on A100 FP16}}$$ Below: memory-bound. Above: compute-bound. The roofline model is the single most useful tool for prioritizing GPU kernel optimization.

slides.title: Tensor cores and FLOPS
slides.body:
Modern GPUs (A100, H100, B200) have **tensor cores** — specialized matrix-multiply units that do small block matmuls in a single cycle. Numbers worth knowing for an H100 SXM:

- bf16 matmul: ~989 TFLOPS
- fp8 matmul: ~1979 TFLOPS
- fp32 (CUDA cores, no tensor cores): ~67 TFLOPS

That's a ~15× ratio between matmul on tensor cores and matmul on CUDA cores. Two consequences:

- **Use the tensor cores.** That means reduced precision (bf16, fp16, fp8) for matmuls. PyTorch + cuDNN do this automatically when you use `autocast`.
- **Tensor core matmuls have shape constraints.** Dimensions should be multiples of 16 (bf16) or 32 (fp8). A model with `d_model = 768` (multiple of 16) hits the fast path; `d_model = 1000` does not, and quietly leaves performance on the table.

**Compute-bound vs memory-bound.** A kernel is compute-bound when it spends most of its time doing arithmetic (e.g. large matmul); memory-bound when it spends most of its time loading bytes from HBM (e.g. softmax over a long sequence). Profilers (Nsight, `torch.profiler`) tell you which regime you're in.

slides.title: HBM, bandwidth, and the memory wall
slides.body:
HBM (high-bandwidth memory) is the GPU's main pool — typically 40 / 80 / 192 GB on modern accelerators. Bandwidth from HBM to the SMs caps how fast data can move:

- A100 80GB: ~2 TB/s
- H100 80GB: ~3.35 TB/s
- H100 NVL (94 GB): ~3.9 TB/s

This matters because a deep network's runtime decomposes into compute + memory traffic. Roofline analysis: a kernel's max throughput is `min(peak_FLOPS, bandwidth × arithmetic_intensity)`. If your arithmetic intensity (FLOPS per byte loaded) is below the ridge, you're memory-bound.

For a typical transformer block:
- Matmuls (Q, K, V projections, FFN) are compute-bound on a long context.
- Attention softmax + LayerNorm + activation are memory-bound.
- The memory-bound ops can dominate runtime if they're not fused with adjacent compute.

**FlashAttention** is the canonical example: rearrange the attention computation to fuse softmax with the matmul, reducing HBM round-trips from `O(N²)` to `O(N)`. Same arithmetic, very different runtime.

question.question: Your training loop is at 30% MFU (model FLOPs utilization). What's the most likely cause to investigate first?
options: Your model is too small to saturate the GPU

Memory-bound ops dominate runtime — check the profiler for time spent in softmax, layernorm, or unfused elementwise kernels, and look at HBM bandwidth utilization. The matmuls might be fast but you're paying for memory traffic between them
Your batch size is too large
question.explanation: 30% MFU on a modern GPU usually means memory traffic, not compute. The matmuls are likely already on tensor cores; what's eating time is the surrounding ops (norm, activation, attention softmax, copy). Profile and fuse. Smaller batch size helps when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck (better cache reuse); larger doesn't always help.

slides.title: Memory accounting for training
slides.body:
When training a model with `P` parameters in fp16/bf16, the rough memory budget per parameter is:

- **Weights**: 2 bytes (fp16/bf16)
- **Gradients**: 2 bytes (matched precision)
- **Optimizer state (Adam)**: 8 bytes (fp32 momentum + variance)
- **Master weights**: 4 bytes (fp32 copy for stable updates)

Total: **~16 bytes per parameter** for plain mixed-precision training with Adam.

A 1B-parameter model: ~16 GB just for weights+grads+optimizer. An 80GB H100 fits that with room for activations. A 7B-parameter model: ~112 GB — doesn't fit on one H100. You need either:

1. **ZeRO/FSDP**: shard the optimizer state, gradients, weights across GPUs.
2. **Gradient checkpointing**: trade compute for memory by recomputing activations during backward.
3. **CPU offload**: stash optimizer state on the host, pull as needed.
4. **Lower precision**: fp8 matmuls cut weights+grads to 1 byte each.

Activations are extra and depend on `(batch, seq_len, layers, hidden)`. For a 7B model at seq_len 8K with batch 1, activations alone can be 20-40 GB. Gradient checkpointing reduces this dramatically (10-20%) at the cost of one extra forward pass per step.

slides.title: Why this matters in practice
slides.body:
Three failure modes that all stem from GPU illiteracy:

**1. Silent slowdowns.** Use a non-multiple-of-16 hidden dimension and your tensor cores fall off the fast path. The model trains; you just paid 2× more compute than you needed to. The training script doesn't print an error.

**2. OOM at sequence length you didn't expect.** Activations grow with `O(batch × seq_len × layers × hidden)`. Doubling seq_len from 4K to 8K can quadruple activation memory because attention activations are quadratic in seq_len (without FlashAttention). Now you understand why FlashAttention's linear-memory claim matters.

**3. Inference throughput collapses at long context.** A 7B model serving 128K context spends most of its time in attention rather than FFN. The KV cache alone is multiple GB. If your serving framework doesn't use PagedAttention (vLLM-style), throughput at long context will be 5-10× worse than at short context.

You'll see all three on the systems path. Each is grounded in the bandwidth-vs-compute roofline and the memory accounting above. Build the muscle to read a profiler trace and you can diagnose any of them in minutes.

question.question: Why does Adam optimizer state cost 8 bytes per parameter even when weights are bf16?
options: Adam needs 8 bytes for arithmetic precision

Adam stores per-parameter momentum (m) and variance (v), each typically in fp32 to avoid numerical drift over thousands of updates. Two fp32 values = 8 bytes. Fp16 momentum is unstable; the standard mixed-precision recipe keeps optimizer state in fp32
question.explanation: Standard mixed-precision keeps optimizer state in fp32 because the running averages can accumulate large dynamic range over training. Cutting Adam to fp16 has been explored (8-bit Adam, AdaFactor, Lion) but isn't the default in PyTorch. ZeRO/FSDP shards this state across GPUs so the per-GPU cost stays manageable.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
Now you have the substrate. Next lessons drill into how training and serving exploit it:

- [[mixed-precision]] — what each precision actually buys you
- [[data-parallelism]] — synchronizing gradients across GPUs
- [[fsdp]] — sharding state when the model doesn't fit
- [[vllm]] — turning a checkpoint into a high-throughput service

Key takeaways:
- Tensor cores do matmul fast at reduced precision; CUDA cores are 10-15× slower
- HBM bandwidth caps memory-bound kernels (softmax, layernorm); compute is rarely the limit on small ops
- Adam training memory: ~16 bytes per parameter (weights + grads + optimizer state)
- FlashAttention, FSDP, gradient checkpointing all attack different parts of the same memory wall
- MFU < 50% almost always means memory traffic, not compute

slides.title: Bandwidth, not FLOPs, is usually the limit
slides.body:
An A100 SXM has roughly **312 TFLOPS** of FP16 tensor-core throughput and **2.0 TB/s** of HBM2e bandwidth.

Naive arithmetic: each FP16 element is 2 bytes, so the GPU can READ at $2.0\text{ TB/s} / 2 = 10^{12}$ elements/s. To keep the tensor cores busy at 312 TFLOPS, each element loaded from HBM needs to participate in ~300 FLOPs — i.e., the **arithmetic intensity** must exceed ~150 FLOPs/byte.

Matrix multiplies have intensity proportional to the contraction dimension, so a big GEMM (say $K\!=\!4096$) is compute-bound. An elementwise add is memory-bound — it does 1 FLOP per 8 bytes (read A, read B, write C) and runs at HBM bandwidth, ~5% of peak FLOPs.

Knowing which side you're on tells you what optimization will help: fusion + tiling for memory-bound code, picking a bigger GEMM shape for compute-bound code.

question.question: A 4096×4096 × 4096×4096 FP16 matmul does $2 \cdot 4096^3 \approx 1.37\times 10^{11}$ FLOPs and reads ~$2\cdot 2 \cdot 4096^2 = 6.7\times 10^{7}$ bytes. What's its arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte, to the nearest 100)?
question.hint: Intensity = FLOPs / bytes. Drop the cancelling factors carefully.

question.question: When does a Tensor Core deliver a speedup over a CUDA core for the same matmul?
options: Always — it is just a faster CUDA core.
When the operation is a small-precision dense matmul with shapes that match the TC tile size.
question.explanation: Tensor Cores execute small 4×4 or 16×16 mixed-precision matmul tiles in a single instruction. They light up on FP16/BF16/INT8/FP8 GEMMs whose dimensions are multiples of the TC tile (commonly 8 or 16). At FP64 or for non-GEMM kernels they sit idle and CUDA cores do the work.

hints: Tensor cores are specialized matmul units — what is special about them?
If a dimension is 7 wide instead of 8, padding makes the TC operate sub-peak.
slides.workedSolution: TCs execute small fixed-shape MMA instructions in low precision. They beat CUDA cores when (a) the op is dense matmul, (b) operands are FP16/BF16/INT8/FP8, and (c) the shape is a multiple of the TC tile size (typically 8 or 16). Outside those conditions — FP64 work, irregular kernels, off-shape dimensions — CUDA cores carry the load.

question.question: Compute-bound or memory-bound?
question.prompt: Your training profile shows tensor-core utilization at 12%, HBM read bandwidth saturated at ~95% of peak. Which side is the bottleneck, and which class of optimization should you reach for first?
Explain, in your own words, why 'arithmetic intensity' is the right way to predict whether a kernel will benefit from a faster GPU vs. faster memory.
question.rubric: Mentions the roofline model intuition: low intensity = bandwidth-bound (faster FLOPs won't help); high intensity = compute-bound (faster bandwidth won't help).

objectives: Distinguish SM/CUDA-core/Tensor-core throughput and what each is for.
Reason about HBM bandwidth as a first-order constraint on training speed.
Estimate whether a kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound.
